analysis.one_liner: Freezes new IRS enforcement funding until the agency submits a spending plan Congress can veto.
analysis.headline: All 17 Senate Republican backers saw the bill die in the Finance Committee without a hearing or vote when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act gave the IRS long-term funding, including money for enforcement — audits and collections aimed largely at underreported income. This bill would have frozen most of that enforcement money for at least 60 days while the IRS wrote a detailed multi-year spending plan, and would have let Congress repeatedly veto the plan, restarting the freeze each time. It also would have required quarterly spending reports, with the IRS losing $1 million of its enforcement money for each day a report was late.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers most exposed to IRS enforcement — concentrated among high-income households and large businesses with complex returns — would benefit from the funding freeze, since delayed audits mean delayed or avoided collections. Supporters also argued ordinary taxpayers would gain from the required public reporting on audit rates by income group and protections against expansion of audit activity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and businesses facing audits

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits obligating most Inflation Reduction Act enforcement funds from enactment until 60 days after the IRS submits a comprehensive spending plan, with funds for clearing return-processing backlogs and reducing call wait times exempted from the freeze.
Congress could enact a joint resolution of disapproval of the IRS spending plan, which would force a new plan and restart another 60-day freeze on the enforcement funds.

The spending plan had to detail audit rates by income group, taxpayer-service performance, and multi-year objectives, reviewed by the Comptroller General, the National Taxpayer Advocate, and the Office of Management and Budget — a level of disclosure the IRS did not previously owe Congress in this form.

The IRS and Treasury would have to file quarterly reports on every expenditure and hire, with automatic funding reductions of $1 million per day (and smaller amounts for Treasury accounts) for each day a required report was late.

analysis.who_pays: The freeze would delay audits and collections of taxes already owed, and uncollected taxes are ultimately made up by compliant taxpayers — primarily wage earners whose taxes are withheld automatically — or show up as larger deficits. The IRS itself would lose enforcement capacity during each freeze and face funding penalties for late reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Compliant taxpayers and the IRS itself

drawbacks.text: The bill's core mechanism — a 60-day freeze on enforcement money that Congress could extend indefinitely through repeated disapproval resolutions — would delay audits and collections of taxes already owed, with no assurance the delayed work ever happens.

The automatic penalties are steep and mechanical: $10 million per day for a late annual plan, $1 million per day for a late IRS quarterly report, and fixed daily reductions for late Treasury reports, cutting money from the same enforcement accounts the bill puts under a freeze.

The reporting requirements are extensive — audit breakdowns by income group and audit type, per-hire descriptions, fair-collection violation tracking — and would consume agency resources to produce, which an honest supporter would weigh against the transparency they buy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is real value in what the bill demanded: a public, itemized accounting of how Inflation Reduction Act enforcement money is spent, including audit rates broken out by income, addresses a genuine fairness concern about who gets audited. But the bill's dominant lever was not transparency — it was the freeze-plus-disapproval structure, which could keep enforcement money locked up indefinitely. That structure mainly reduced enforcement risk for the taxpayers most likely to face audits, at the cost of delaying collection of taxes already owed, with the shortfall borne by everyone else. A reporting bill without the freeze would have been a materially different and easier-to-defend proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on November 16, 2022, joined by 15 Republican original cosponsors; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind in its history.

The bill would have frozen most Inflation Reduction Act enforcement funds for at least 60 days pending a detailed IRS spending plan, exempting only funds for eliminating return-processing backlogs and reducing call wait times.
Under the bill, Congress could disapprove the spending plan by joint resolution, forcing a new plan and another 60-day freeze, and the IRS would have faced daily funding reductions for late reports.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the IRS's multi-year enforcement and service funding under the Inflation Reduction Act continued without any freeze or congressional veto mechanism. The 17 Republican senators who backed the bill did not get the spending-plan process they sought, and the taxpayers with the most audit exposure — concentrated at the top of the income scale — got no relief from it.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its freeze-and-disapproval structure for Inflation Reduction Act enforcement funds.

for.name: 16 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the entire bill's support come from the Republican conference.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee of referral; held no hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; the referral was the only action in the bill's history.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.role: 48 Democrats and 2 independents holding Senate control
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it received no committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 17 sponsors and cosponsors was a Republican, and the Democratic majority took no action on it — a clean party split, with no Democrats or independents supporting the bill in the record.

industries.note: The enforcement funding the bill would freeze is aimed at underreported income, which is concentrated among high earners and complex business returns, so the freeze would mainly delay their audit and collection exposure. Taxes that go uncollected shift onto compliant taxpayers or the deficit, making this a gain for them at the public's cost. This describes the bill if it had passed; it never did.
